activity.title: I am excited to share that I will be joining LinkedIn as a Software Engineer Intern this upcoming summer in Mountain View, California!

Everyone wants cheaper compute. Decentralized infrastructure has it. Actually using it is the hard part. Julius Zhou and I built Necto to fix that, and we won $4K at ETHDenver . Necto is a compute marketplace that turns plain English requests into compliant GPU deployments, routing workloads across decentralized and institutional providers while automatically handling provisioning, payments, and audit logs through an agent. Necto makes DePIN accessible to everyone. We ended up taking home 3 awards: ADI Foundation Prize ($2k) Finalist for Futurllama ($1k) Celebrity Judge Honorable Mention ($1k) Huge shoutout to Grace Reginato , Eli Dubizh , Siya Jariwala , Neena Naikar , Gemini , and Boiler Blockchain for flying us out and putting together an incredible hacker house. Being surrounded by that level of talent and energy for the week created the perfect environment to just put our heads down and build. 40 hours. 3 incredible teammates. A mountain of energy drinks. And just about zero sleep. The result? We won at Cal Hacks 2025! Our team took home $2,000 for the Best Use of Sui prize at the world's largest collegiate hackathon, competing against 3,000+ of the brightest minds. I couldn't have done it without my brilliant teammates: Haotian Li , Dhiyaan Nirmal , and Akash Mishra . The big problem in the decentralized world? 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱. Communities are stuck on platforms like Discord and Telegram where they have no data ownership, and even simple interactions are fragmented across apps. Our answer is 𝗢𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿. Otter is a unified, decentralized hub for communication and commerce. No more switching apps. No more giving up your data. Otter brings 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 into one place. You can automatically copy the strategies of expert traders or ask our AI copilot for guidance using natural language. We also enabled users to create and manage secure, token gated DAO communities. All communication is protected through encrypted, on-chain messaging, and a live activity stream keeps you informed of network wide actions. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸? Sui Move (smart contracts), React, Typescript, Supabase, Fetch.ai , Gemini A massive thank you to Daniel Leavitt and the Sui Foundation for all the support during the hackathon, and to Mysten Labs for sponsoring our travels. Honored to share that I won 1st Place in the Gold Track at Purdue's Hello World 2025 This past weekend, I had the incredible opportunity to compete at Hello World 2025, one of Purdue’s largest hackathons. I built Cashly in just 24 hours and took home 1st Place in the Gold Track out of 400+ participants and 130+ projects! Cashly is a personal finance platform designed to help students manage their money effortlessly. It automatically tracks spending, income, and investments, categorizes transactions, provides trends and insights, allows goal setting with visual progress, and delivers personalized financial advice using Plaid for secure bank integration and LLaMA AI. The goal was to make managing money simple, insightful, and even a little fun, turning a stressful task into an empowering experience for students. The project involved full-stack development: React + TypeScript and Tailwind CSS for the frontend, Convex for backend data storage, real time updates, and authentication, Python services for PDF parsing and AI insights, and integrations with Plaid and Alpha Vantage for live bank and stock data. From handling OAuth flows and banking updates to building interactive dashboards, it was truly incredibly rewarding to see it all come together. Huge thank you to Tanay Gondil and all the Hello World Organizers for creating such an amazing event, and to the Purdue community for the support throughout the weekend. I'm excited to take this experience into the next hackathon, where I hope to create something bigger, better, and even more impactful. As my internship at LinkedIn wraps up in the next couple weeks, I wanted to take the time to reflect on my experiences and growth this summer. This summer, I worked on LinkedIn's Python Infrastructure team where I helped build an AI-powered autofixer that automatically converts Linkedin's Python services to safe async patterns, optimizing a previously tedious and error-prone migration across thousands of services. This internship taught me that software engineering ≠ coding. With the rise of agentic coding, many developers (including myself) have wondered what the future of software engineering looks like. But some of my biggest lessons this summer came from everything surrounding the code: navigating massive codebases, familiarizing myself with foreign systems, and making design decisions with real tradeoffs. I learned that great engineering isn't about just writing clean code, but also involves understanding the problem and designing the right solution. A big thank you to my tech lead Friedrich Ewald and manager Kaiyang Zheng for giving me the opportunity to contribute to a high impact initiative at LinkedIn and encouraging me to stay curious as I grow as an engineer. I'd like to also thank the rest of my intern pod, Anson Lam , Grace Jin , Emma Bennett for working alongside me, I couldn't have asked for a better group to learn, brainstorm, and navigate through the summer. Last but not least, a huge shout out to my recruiter Jeffery C. and the rest of the intern program team for planning super fun events that made this summer unforgettable! #LinkedInterns

National [In]tern Day was incredible! 💙 We kicked things off with a hackathon. My teammates, HariChandana Srikurmum , Jeremy Merino , and Anson Lam , and I proposed and built LinkedIn Coffee Chat, a feature that connects you with someone outside your network who shares common interests for a one-on-one video conversation. We asked ourselves “How can networking feel more authentic?” That question drove our brainstorming, helped us define the product flow and user experience, and led us to build a working proof of concept. Using GitHub Copilot, we turned our ideas into code at a blazing speed. It felt like having a superpowered engineer bring our spec to life. After building, we played just as hard. From rock climbing and mini golf to DIY bag, portrait photoshoots, and karaoke, there were so many activities planned for interns throughout the day. It was great to reconnect with fellow interns I hadn't seen much because we've all been busy getting s**t done and to meet plenty of new friends. 🎉 he more time I spend at LinkedIn, the more [in]describably fulfilled I feel. Grateful for the inspiring people around me and an internship that's challenging, collaborative, and fun. #NationalInternDay #LinkedIn #LinkedInterns #LinkedInLife #TechInternship

Won the JacHacks hackathon in San Francisco yesterday with Umang Sharma , Arshmeet Sodhi and Aswath Jacob , in the open track! we built Recall, smart glasses that remember the people you meet, because sometimes we don't. it runs on the new Meta Ray-Ban glasses with the display, so everything shows up right in your vision. when you talk to someone it listens, catches who they are and what they're working on, and saves it. next time you see them, facial recognition pulls their card back up so you have context and don't have to start from scratch. also has a dashboard on the mobile app to see everyone you met and search to find conversations. under the hood it's built on Jac, a really cool language, where your whole network is a graph. the glasses handle the face and the speech, and Jac does the remembering. the motive was two things. one, for people with alzheimer's and dementia, so faces and names don't slip away. two, for networking, when you meet 278092583 people in a day and remember none of them. got to meet and work with prof. Jason Mars too. loved his energy and humility. made some good connections and friends along the way. really enjoyed the whole thing. would recommend.

I kept rebuilding the same front-end pieces for multiple side projects and couldn’t find an existing library that fit what I needed. It was either a UI-only component library or a separate charts library, never both and never tailored for LLM-driven workflows. So I built a Claude-friendly component library that includes an MCP server and a design system that Claude—or other LLMs—can use directly. I hooked the MCP server into my global Claude instructions, so whenever I spin up a web interface it automatically references the design system and the components I’ve created. The result lets me put dashboards and other web apps together much faster. Have fun and let me know what you think. Source code & playground here: https://lnkd.in/gUVGuNPd
